summary:
Necosphere – Earth System Trend Exploration Platform

The project name combines neko (ねこ), the Japanese word for cat, with eco-sphere, representing Earth as a globe. This name reflects the project's geographical focus and its interactive spherical representation of the planet. Necosphere is the platform developed by PCCAT for exploring environmental measurements and investigating changes across Earth's systems. Together, the name reflects our team's identity and connection to technology.

We developed an interactive geo-spatial platform that brings together 15 environmental variables, covering precipitation, water resources, vegetation, soil, tree characteristics, atmospheric gases and snow conditions.

Necosphere addresses NASA's Be An Earth System Trend Detective! challenge by allowing users to explore environmental data through an interactive 3D globe or 2D map. Users can select variables, choose dates or periods, view geographical patterns through color-coded visualizations and export available data for further analysis.

Our project makes complex environmental information easier to explore, encourages scientific investigation and raises awareness of Earth's interconnected systems. We aim to make Earth observation more accessible to students, educators, researchers and the wider public.

PCCAT turns environmental data into discovery and curiosity into exploration!

Introduction

Most people would think ‘The Next Frontier’ is about looking out into space and onto further and further worlds, but advances in technology also allow us to look inward, at our only home

1. System Overview

Necosphere is an interactive geo-spatial environmental data visualization and exploration platform.

Its central purpose is to make environmental measurements easier to investigate by combining geographical interfaces, dataset selection, temporal exploration, charts, statistical analysis and export functionality.

The system can be understood through five main components.

A. Geographical Visualization

The platform provides a three-dimensional globe and a two-dimensional map. These views allow users to explore the geographical context of environmental observations.

B. Environmental Data Management

The platform organizes the prepared environmental datasets into a library. Users can search for and select available datasets and variables.

C. Temporal and Geographical Exploration

Users can define time windows and geographical filters to examine selected environmental measurements within a particular period or area.

D. Data Analysis and Comparison

Charts, trend analysis, rate-of-change calculations, and regional or temporal comparisons provide additional ways to investigate the selected observations.

E. Data Import and Export

Users can import supported local datasets and export available information from their investigations for further analysis.

Together, these components make Necosphere more than a geographical visualization tool. It provides an environment for exploring environmental observations and investigating patterns within the available data.

2. Environmental Variables

Necosphere incorporates 15 environmental variables representing different components of Earth's systems.

These variables are organized into 11 data collections in the website. Related variables may be grouped within the same collection.

A. Precipitation and Water Resources

1) Rainfall / Precipitation

Rainfall measures the amount of water falling from the atmosphere to the Earth's surface over a particular period.

It is an important environmental measurement for understanding precipitation patterns, seasonal changes, drought conditions and water availability.

2) Terrestrial Water Storage

Terrestrial water storage represents water stored across land-based environments.

This includes water held in soil, groundwater, rivers, lakes, reservoirs and other terrestrial storage systems.

Changes in terrestrial water storage can provide information about water availability and the behaviour of land-based water resources.

B. Vegetation and Land Surface Conditions

3) Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI)

NDVI is a vegetation index derived from remotely sensed measurements.

It is used to estimate vegetation greenness and assess vegetation conditions.

NDVI can help identify geographical differences in vegetation and support investigations into vegetation growth, degradation and seasonal changes.

4) Ground Surface Temperature

Ground surface temperature describes the temperature of the Earth's surface.

It provides information about how different geographical locations heat and cool over time.

It can be used to investigate surface temperature patterns and variations in land-surface heating.

C. Soil Conditions

5) Soil Temperature

Soil temperature measures thermal conditions within the soil.

It influences plant growth, soil biological activity, nutrient cycling and the movement of moisture through soil.

6) Soil Moisture

Soil moisture measures the amount of water contained in soil.

It is important for understanding agricultural conditions, vegetation health, drought development and water availability.

7) Soil Electrical Conductivity

Soil electrical conductivity measures the ability of soil to conduct electrical current.

It is influenced by soil properties, including the presence of dissolved salts.

It can therefore provide information relevant to soil salinity, agricultural conditions and soil characteristics.

D. Tree Characteristics and Conditions

8) Tree Height and Diameter

Tree height and diameter describe the physical dimensions of trees.

Tree height measures the vertical extent of a tree, while diameter measures the thickness of its trunk.

These measurements help characterize tree development and forest structure.

9) Tree Apparent Dielectric Permittivity

Tree apparent dielectric permittivity describes the apparent dielectric properties of tree material.

It relates to how tree tissues interact with electromagnetic fields and can provide information relevant to the physical and water-related properties of vegetation.

10) Tree Temperature

Tree temperature measures the thermal conditions of trees or their measured surfaces.

It can help investigate how vegetation responds to environmental conditions and temperature variations.

E. Atmospheric Conditions

11) Atmospheric Gas Concentrations

Atmospheric gas concentrations describe the amounts of selected gases present in the atmosphere.

Depending on the gases represented in the dataset, these measurements can support investigations into atmospheric composition and environmental processes.

F. Coastal and Aquatic Conditions

12) Coastal Water Quality — Chlorophyll-a

Chlorophyll-a is a pigment found in photosynthetic organisms, particularly phytoplankton.

Its concentration in coastal waters is commonly used as an indicator of phytoplankton abundance.

It can provide insights into aquatic ecosystem conditions and variations in coastal water quality.

G. Snow and Cryosphere Conditions

13) Snow Density

Snow density describes the mass of snow contained within a given volume.

It provides information about snowpack characteristics, compaction and the amount of water stored in snow.

14) Snow Temperature

Snow temperature describes thermal conditions within a snowpack.

It can help investigate freezing and melting processes and changes in snow conditions.

15) Snow Stratigraphy

Snow stratigraphy describes the arrangement and characteristics of different layers within a snowpack.

It provides information about snowpack structure, accumulation history and the development of individual snow layers.

3. Environmental Data Preparation

The environmental datasets used in Necosphere were prepared and cleaned before being incorporated into the platform.

This preparation provides a more organized foundation for visualization and analysis.

Environmental datasets can differ significantly in their original structure. They may contain different column names, measurement units, date formats, geographical references and missing-value conventions.

Data preparation is therefore an important part of the project.

The general preparation process includes:

1. Identifying the original environmental datasets.

2. Examining their structures and available measurements.

3. Organising the relevant variables.

4. Preparing the data into formats suitable for the platform.

5. Cleaning and organizing records where necessary.

6. Preserving available temporal information.

7. Examining the information associated with each dataset.

8. Preparing the resulting data for visualization and exploration.

The prepared datasets form the scientific foundation of the platform.

The interpretation of each dataset depends on the information actually available in its source. Measurements from individual stations, study sites, grid cells or larger summaries should be understood according to their original coverage.

4. Interactive Globe and Map Implementation

The geographical interface is an important component of Necosphere.

The globe implementation uses a custom rendering approach based on JavaScript and browser graphics technologies.

The implementation processes geographical polygon data and transforms it into a representation suitable for drawing a spherical globe and a flat geographical map.

4.1 HTML Canvas

The globe interface is hosted inside an HTML canvas element.

The canvas provides the drawing surface used by the JavaScript rendering implementation.

The implementation adjusts the canvas dimensions using the browser's device pixel ratio to support higher-resolution rendering on different displays.

4.2 Canvas 2D Rendering

The active rendering path uses the browser's Canvas 2D API.

The implementation obtains a two-dimensional rendering context from the canvas and uses drawing operations to construct the geographical representation.

The rendering process uses paths, transformations, clipping, fills and strokes to draw land geometry and geographical grid lines.

4.3 Geographical Coordinate Processing

The implementation loads the ne_110m_land.geojson file.

The GeoJSON land polygons contain geographical coordinates expressed as longitude and latitude.

The JavaScript code processes these coordinates and creates corresponding two-dimensional and three-dimensional representations.

The three-dimensional representation uses unit-sphere vectors generated from geographical coordinates.

This allows geographical points to be projected and tested against the viewing direction of the globe.

4.4 Custom Projection and Visibility Calculations

The globe implementation includes custom mathematical functions for representing geographical positions in three-dimensional space and projecting them onto the viewing surface.

Vector operations are used for calculations involving:

• Three-dimensional positions.

• Camera orientation.

• Viewing direction.

• Geographical projection.

• Visibility and horizon calculations.

• Transformation between geographical and display coordinates.

The implementation also inserts intermediate points along sufficiently long polygon segments. This improves the representation of polygon boundaries during spherical projection.

4.5 Globe Rendering

The globe view is drawn using the processed geographical polygons.

The renderer calculates the visible land and sea regions according to the current viewing position.

It also draws geographical grid lines at regular angular intervals.

The rendering uses separate land, water and outline colors.

4.6 Two-Dimensional Map Rendering

The implementation includes a flat geographical rendering mode.

The geographical coordinates are transformed into a flat map representation, allowing the same underlying land geometry to be displayed without the spherical perspective.

The implementation also handles longitude wrapping so that geographical features crossing the map's horizontal boundaries can be displayed correctly.

4.7 Transition Between Globe and Map

The interface includes a transition control that switches between the globe and two-dimensional geographical representations.

The implementation maintains a transition state and updates the rendering over successive animation frames.

The transition gradually changes the geographical projection between the spherical and flat representations.

4.8 User Interaction and Motion

The globe implementation supports interactive navigation through mouse, pointer, touch and wheel events.

Its interaction mechanisms include:

• Mouse dragging.

• Pointer movement.

• Touch-based movement.

• Two-finger interaction.

• Scroll-wheel zoom adjustment.

• Touch-based zoom adjustment.

• Smooth changes to the viewing position and distance.

The implementation uses motion smoothing and an animation loop to produce gradual updates during interaction.

4.9 Human Development Contribution

Most of the sphere-rendering implementation was written by a human developer.

The custom coordinate processing, vector mathematics, projection logic, geographical drawing and interaction mechanisms form a substantial part of the manually developed rendering implementation.

5. Main Website Features

Feature 1: Interactive Three-Dimensional Globe

Necosphere provides an interactive three-dimensional representation of Earth.

Users can rotate and navigate the globe to explore geographical locations and view the spatial context of environmental information.

The globe provides a spherical perspective that makes it easier to understand the relationship between different geographical areas.

Feature 2: Two-Dimensional Map

The platform also provides a flat geographical representation of Earth.

The map provides an alternative view for examining geographical information and environmental patterns.

Users can switch between the globe and map representations depending on their exploration needs.

Feature 3: Globe-to-Map Transition

Users can transition between the three-dimensional globe and two-dimensional map.

The transition allows users to move between different geographical representations without leaving the exploration environment.

Feature 4: Environmental Dataset Library

The website organizes its prepared environmental data into a library containing 11 data collections.

These collections provide access to the environmental measurements incorporated into the platform.

Related variables may be grouped within the same collection, which is why the number of collections differs from the total number of documented environmental variables.

Feature 5: Dataset Search and Variable Selection

Users can search the available datasets and select the environmental variable they want to investigate.

The selected dataset determines which measurements and associated information are available for geographical visualization and analysis.

Feature 6: Date and Time Window Selection

Environmental measurements change over time.

Necosphere provides date and time window controls that allow users to select the period they want to investigate.

The available dates depend on the temporal coverage of the selected dataset.

This allows users to explore different periods and examine the corresponding observations.

Feature 7: Geographical Filtering

The platform provides geographical filters for narrowing an investigation to a selected area.

Available filtering options include geographical region selection and latitude/longitude bounds.

These filters allow users to focus their exploration on particular geographical areas rather than always examining the complete dataset.

Feature 8: Color-Coded Geographical Visualization

Environmental observations are represented geographically using color-coded visualizations.

Different colors correspond to different values or value ranges within the selected dataset.

This helps users identify geographical differences and patterns.

The interpretation of colors depends on the selected variable and its visualization scale.

The platform also preserves missing information rather than treating missing observations as measured values.

Feature 9: Observation Inspection

Users can interact with displayed geographical information to inspect available measurements.

Selecting or tapping a mapped observation allows the user to examine the associated value where the dataset provides an identifiable observation.

This helps connect the geographical visualization with the underlying environmental measurement.

Feature 10: Charts and Graphical Exploration

Necosphere provides chart-based exploration of environmental measurements.

Charts provide another way to investigate observations and understand how values vary across the selected period.

The available chart options include:

• Warming rate.

• Then-to-now comparison.

• Year explorer.

• Variability exploration.

These chart views provide different perspectives on the selected environmental data.

Feature 11: Trend Analysis

The platform includes analytical tools for investigating changes in environmental measurements over time.

Trend analysis helps users explore whether a selected measurement exhibits an increasing or decreasing pattern across the available observations.

The platform includes rate-of-change analysis and exploratory uncertainty calculations.

The rate-map analysis requires at least 10 annual values.

The exploratory uncertainty analysis requires 20 consecutive annual values and non-zero residual variation.

These requirements are important because statistical trend analysis needs an adequate temporal record.

The current built-in datasets do not meet the 20-year requirement at each site for the exploratory uncertainty calculation.

Where the requirements are not met, the platform should not present the unavailable analysis as though it were statistically supported.

Feature 12: Statistical Uncertainty and Significance Exploration

The platform includes exploratory uncertainty calculations using 95% Newey-West intervals.

It also provides optional Benjamini–Yekutieli false discovery rate correction.

These features help users examine uncertainty and multiple-testing considerations when interpreting trends.

However, these calculations should be interpreted carefully.

The exploratory 95% intervals are not NASA instrument uncertainty or model uncertainty.

The associated p-values are exploratory and asymptotic. They should not be treated as definitive proof of an environmental effect.

The platform does not establish causal relationships from statistical associations.

Feature 13: Regional Comparison

The platform allows users to compare environmental information across geographical regions.

Regional comparisons can help users investigate differences between selected areas and examine how environmental measurements vary geographically.

Regional means are calculated as unweighted means of available observations.

They should not be interpreted as area-weighted global or regional estimates.

Feature 14: Early and Recent Period Comparison

Users can compare different time periods to investigate changes between earlier and more recent observations.

This makes it possible to examine how selected environmental measurements differ between the chosen periods.

Such comparisons can provide useful context for investigating environmental change.

Feature 15: Data Table

The website provides an accessible data table for examining the underlying values associated with the selected dataset and filters.

The table complements the geographical and chart visualisations by presenting information in a structured format.

Feature 16: Read-Summary Functionality

The platform includes a read-summary feature that uses browser speech capabilities to read the available summary.

This provides an additional way for users to access information presented by the website.

Feature 17: Local Dataset Import

Users can import their own local datasets into the platform.

The supported import formats include:

• CSV.

• GeoJSON.

• Excel (.xlsx).

The import functionality allows users to explore compatible external datasets in addition to the built-in environmental collections.

The processing of imported files takes place locally in the browser.

Imported files are not uploaded to or stored by the platform's server.

The documented import limits include:

• CSV and GeoJSON: up to 10 MB and 50,000 rows.

• Excel: up to 200 MB, processed locally.

Imported data is temporary and is lost when the page is refreshed. Users who reopen a saved investigation must import the relevant local file again.

Feature 18: Data and Visuazisation Export

Necosphere provides export functionality for obtaining information from an investigation.

Available export options include:

• Full dataset export.

• Filtered CSV export.

• Map values CSV export.

• Graph SVG export.

• Comparison CSV export.

• Settings JSON export.

These options allow users to preserve data, charts, comparison results and investigation settings for further examination or reporting.

Feature 19: Copy View Link

The platform provides a way to copy a link to the current built-in view.

This allows users to share or reopen a particular platform view and its associated settings.

Feature 20: Saved Investigations

Users can save investigations so that their selected settings can be preserved.

Saved investigations retain the relevant exploration settings.

For investigations involving locally imported files, the original file must be imported again when needed because imported files are not permanently stored by the platform.

Feature 21: Place Search

The platform includes place search functionality to help users locate geographical areas of interest.

This supports geographical exploration by allowing users to navigate to a relevant location.

Feature 22: Interface Preferences and Accessibility

Necosphere provides interface preferences that support different user needs.

These include:

• Reduced-motion preferences.

• Larger text.

• Interface settings.

These options help make the platform more comfortable and accessible to a wider range of users.

6. General System Workflow

A typical Necosphere investigation follows the process below.

Step 1: Access the website

The user opens https://necosphere.pages.dev

Step 2: Explore the geographical interface

The user views the globe or two-dimensional map and navigates to an area of interest.

Step 3: Search or select a dataset

The user searches the environmental data library and selects the dataset or variable to investigate.

Step 4: Define the time period

The user selects the date or time window relevant to the investigation.

Step 5: Apply geographical filters

Where necessary, the user selects a geographical region or defines latitude and longitude bounds.

Step 6: Examine the geographical visualisation

The platform displays the available observations using geographical and colour-coded representations.

Step 7: Inspect observations

The user selects displayed observations to examine their associated values.

Step 8: Explore charts and tables

The user examines the data through charts and the accessible data table.

Step 9: Investigate trends

Where the selected dataset meets the relevant requirements, the user explores rates of change and statistical trend information.

Step 10: Compare regions or periods

The user compares geographical areas or different time periods to investigate differences in environmental measurements.

Step 11: Export or save the investigation

The user exports available datasets, charts, comparisons or saves the investigation for later use.

7. Benefits and Expected Impact

1) Improved Access to Environmental Information

Necosphere brings multiple environmental datasets into one interactive environment, making them easier to discover and explore.

2) Improved Geographical Understanding

The combination of three-dimensional and two-dimensional geographical views provides alternative ways to understand the locations and distributions of environmental observations.

3) Exploration of Multiple Earth Systems

The platform covers 15 environmental variables representing different components of Earth's systems.

This allows users to investigate vegetation, soil, water, atmospheric, tree, coastal and snow-related conditions.

4) Better Understanding of Temporal Patterns

Date selection, charts, and temporal comparisons allow users to examine how environmental measurements vary over time.

5) Support for Environmental Trend Exploration

Trend analysis and rate-of-change tools provide additional ways to investigate long-term environmental behavior where sufficient observations are available.

6) Geographical Comparison

Regional filtering and comparison features help users investigate differences between geographical areas.

7) More Accessible Scientific Information

Interactive maps, charts, tables and read-summary functionality provide different ways to engage with environmental information.

8) Support for Further Analysis

Data imports and exports allow users to work with external datasets and continue analysis outside the platform.

9) Responsible Interpretation of Environmental Data

By distinguishing between different types of observations, missing values and analytical limitations, the platform supports more careful interpretation of environmental information.

10) Environmental Awareness

Necosphere encourages users to explore environmental measurements and develop a better understanding of the systems that make up Earth.

8. Project Goal

The overall goal of Necosphere is to make Earth system data exploration more accessible, interactive, and informative.

By combining geographical visualization, environmental dataset selection, temporal and geographical filtering, charts, trend analysis, comparisons and data export, the platform provides a unified environment for investigating environmental measurements.

The project aims to help users move beyond simply viewing environmental data and towards exploring patterns, examining changes, comparing observations and understanding the limitations of the available information.

10. Development

During development, our team considered data organization, geographical representation, accessibility, usability, environmental relevance and the importance of preparing and cleaning datasets before visualization. We also analyzed several existing tools related to the challenge to see what the standard is like and what can be improved upon.

We also provide a few fun things: like the ⁠ graph sound ⁠ feature that visualizes the graph (with sound) in an accessible way, and a little something that appears when you click on the icon in the bottom left. What could the Earth be without it?

The platform was built as a web-based solution via HTML/JavaScript/CSS, frameworks and tools selected by our development team. It was a collaborative effort where each of us contributed ideas towards the user interface and general usage workflow to make it beautiful and intuitive.

Instead of looking at all the many ways data can be input, our software uses a simple CSV format to take in a time series; that simplified a lot of the processing involved. The map and globe views were written completely from scratch, by hand, for best performance. The UI was SI assisted, though we extensively directed and iterated over the output to make sure the UI is just the way it's meant to be.

11. Data Interpretation and Limitations

Environmental datasets have different levels of coverage and different observation periods.

For this reason, the platform should not imply that all observations represent continuous geographical surfaces or complete global measurements.

The following limitations are important when interpreting results.

Different Types of Observations

Some measurements represent individual stations or sensors, while others represent grid-cell averages, study-site references, or regional summaries.

Incomplete Coverage

Some datasets cover only specific locations or research areas.

A measurement from one location should not be interpreted as representative of an entire region without appropriate supporting evidence.

Missing Observations

Missing values are not equivalent to zero measurements.

The platform preserves the distinction between missing information and valid zero values where the dataset defines that distinction.

Temporal Coverage

Different datasets cover different periods and observation frequencies.

The available analysis depends on the number and distribution of observations within the selected time window.

Trend Analysis Requirements

Rate maps require at least 10 annual values.

Exploratory uncertainty calculations require 20 consecutive annual values and non-zero residual variation.

The built-in datasets do not currently provide the required 20 consecutive annual values at each site for that uncertainty calculation.

Statistical Interpretation

The platform's exploratory Newey-West intervals and p-values should not be interpreted as NASA instrument uncertainty or definitive statistical proof.

Regional means are unweighted means of available observations rather than area-weighted estimates.

No Causal Attribution

Observed associations and trends do not establish that one environmental variable caused a change in another.

The platform is designed to support exploration and investigation, not to claim causal relationships that the data cannot establish.
